title: Lights
tagline: The ship is dark. Teach it when a room needs light.
briefing: You wake up on the **Meridian**, a cargo ship drifting between stars. Its software was wiped. Every room is dark and the crew are stumbling around.

The ship still knows how to ask one question, many times a second, for every room: *should this room's light be on?* It asks by calling a function named `lightOn` and giving it the room. Whatever your function returns is the answer.
Right now the function always answers `false`. Your job: make the answer good enough to keep the crew safe without draining the ship's power.
starter: // The ship calls this for every room, twice a second.
// `room` looks like: { name: "Cargo", crew: 2, emergency: false }
// Return true to switch the light on, false to switch it off.

steps.title: Turn every light on
text: A function is a named piece of code that gets **inputs** and gives back an **output**. Here the input is `room` and the output is whatever comes after `return`.
The ship calls `lightOn` once for each of its six rooms. Change `false` to `true` and watch the ship.

predict.question: `lightOn` is called once for every room. If it always returns `true`, how many of the six rooms light up?
options: Only rooms with crew in them
predict.explain: The function ignores `room` completely, so every call gets the same answer: `true`. Now look at the power gauge. Six lights cost more than the reactor makes, so the ship is draining. Lighting everything isn't the answer.

hints: Which word comes after `return`? That word is the answer the ship gets.
In JavaScript, the two true-or-false values are written `true` and `false`, without quotes.

steps.title: Light only rooms with crew
text: `room` is an **object**: a bundle of named values. `room.crew` reads the value named `crew`, the number of people in that room.
A comparison like `room.crew > 0` doesn't print anything. It *produces* a value, `true` or `false`, and that value can be returned directly.
Return whether the room has anyone in it. Then click a room on the ship to see exactly what your function was given and what it answered.

predict.question: The Cargo bay is empty, so `room.crew` is `0`. What does `room.crew > 0` produce?
predict.explain: `0 > 0` is a question, and its answer is `false`. Comparisons always produce `true` or `false`, so returning one is exactly the yes/no answer the ship wants.

goal.text: Rooms with crew are lit; empty rooms are dark.

hints: Read the number of people with `room.crew`.
You want `true` when that number is more than zero. Which comparison operator means "more than"?

steps.title: Emergencies need light
text: Alarms go off in empty rooms, and the crew run in to fix them, in the dark. An emergency room must be lit even before anyone arrives.
An `if` runs its block only when its condition is `true`. A `return` inside it answers immediately and **ends the function**: nothing below it runs for that call.
Add a check for `room.emergency` *above* your crew line.

predict.question: Suppose the `if` block were written *below* the line `return room.crew > 0;`. Would the emergency check ever run?
options: Only when there is an emergency
predict.explain: `return` ends the function. Every call returns at the crew line, so code after it is never reached. Order matters: the special case goes first, the general rule last.

goal.text: Emergency rooms are always lit; otherwise rooms with crew are lit.

hints: `room.emergency` is already `true` or `false`, so it can be the condition on its own: `if (room.emergency)`.
Put the whole `if` block on the lines just after `function lightOn(room) {`.

steps.title: The Bridge never goes dark
text: Captain's order: the Bridge holds the navigation displays, so its light stays on even when nobody is there.
Room names are **strings**: text in quotes. `===` asks whether two values are exactly the same. For strings, that includes capital letters.
Add a second special case for the Bridge.

predict.question: What does `"bridge" === "Bridge"` produce?
predict.explain: Strings are compared character by character, and `b` is not the same character as `B`. The ship spells it `"Bridge"`, so match it exactly.

goal.text: The Bridge is always lit, plus everything from before.

hints: It's the same shape as the emergency check: an `if` with `return true;` inside.
Put it next to the emergency check, before the final `return`.

check.text: The ship runs scenarios you haven't seen. Every room must get the right answer.
